title: Michelin's Free 1900 Guide: Why Cities Pay to Be Rated?｜Curio Archive
description:
Michelin gave its guide away free over a century ago. Why do some cities now pay it to come and rate them?
For anyone who sees "Michelin recommended" and never wondered who pays.

From the free 1900 booklet to tourism bodies in Seoul, Thailand, the US and Taiwan. Seoul's roughly 2 billion won is a lawmaker's figure; Thailand's 143.5 million baht is a related promotion budget, not all paid to Michelin; Taiwan's 10-million-plus NT$ first year is a PTS report; the total could not be found and we do not estimate it.

"Anonymous inspectors who pay their own bills" is Michelin's statement. A Korean restaurant owner filed a complaint, Michelin denied it, and we could not find the prosecutors' outcome; this episode does not claim any star was bought. This channel has no partnership with Michelin.

Data as of 2026-10-31
Illustrations are AI-generated.

chapters.open-book: A Tyre Firm's Book, a Minister
chapters.two-years: The US Never Paid, Then Did
chapters.answer: Money to Invite, Money to Dine

t001.text: You know the Michelin Guide: it rates restaurants, up to 3 stars.

t002.text: But it isn't published by a food magazine. It's a tyre company.

t003.text: One claim has gone around for ages: Michelin stars can be bought.

t004.text: July 2026, at Taipei's awards, per the Tourism Administration, the transport minister spoke.

t005.text: Odd. Why does a minister take the stage for a tyre firm's book?

t006.text: Odder still: 100-plus years ago, this book was given away.

t007.text: Yet now, believe it or not, some cities pay it to come rate them.

t008.text: A Korean lawmaker once grilled officials on it; reportedly American cities never paid, which held only two years.

t009.text: So let's talk: how does a booklet once given away get cities to pay it to rate them?

t010.text: And can that star really be bought?

t011.text: I'm a researcher at the archive. To answer this, we go back to France in 1889.

t012.text: Two brothers in Clermont-Ferrand, France, made tyres.

t013.text: Open a tyre shop today and roads are full of cars. Back then?

t014.text: Officially, all of France had fewer than 3,000 cars.

t016.text: The brothers' idea: get people driving more.

t017.text: Drive farther, tyres wear faster, and back you come.

t018.text: So in 1900, the first guide printed 35,000 copies, every one free.

t019.text: Tyre changes, fuel, and where to eat and sleep.

t020.text: That works out to about 12 copies for every car in France.

t021.text: Handed a pile of freebies, would you value it?

t022.text: Odder still, an author of its 100-year history said:

t023.text: No evidence the book sold more tyres.

t024.text: So the first payer is clear: the tyre company itself.

t025.text: I first found this trade silly.

t026.text: And then this free book got used to prop things up.

t027.text: You may know it: Global Views says a garage, the book under a table leg.

t028.text: So how does Michelin tell it?

t029.text: Its website says in 1920, one of the brothers walked into a tyre shop

t030.text: and saw his beloved guide propping a workbench.

t031.text: Its site: an anecdote they still love.

t032.text: Their story. I found no third-party record.

t033.text: Wherever it was, what did they learn?

t034.text: People only respect what they pay for.

t035.text: Honestly, that line could still sell subscriptions.

t036.text: In 1920, a new edition came out at 7 francs. Now you had to pay for it.

t037.text: And more ruthless still: it dropped the paid ads.

t038.text: The payer changed for the first time: from the tyre company to readers like you.

t039.text: It also hired mystery diners who ate out anonymously.

t040.text: Catch: you paid, so why trust what these people judged?

t041.text: Its answer was a star. In 1926, a star began to appear beside good restaurants.

t042.text: Five years on, 0 to 3 stars; five more, criteria went public.

t043.text: Yes, from the first star, it's exactly 100 years now.

t044.text: Today: 2 stars, worth a detour; 3, worth a special journey.

t046.text: To me, it measures the drive.

t048.text: Michelin says: a set of rules.

t049.text: Inspectors are full-time, unlinked to outsiders, incognito.

t050.text: They visit a place many times and pay every bill. All this is what Michelin says.

t051.text: CommonWealth said an inspector visits 250 restaurants a year on average.

t052.text: That's where a star's value starts. But a team like that isn't cheap.

t053.text: One figure: in 2011, the Financial Times reported the guide

t054.text: lost over $24 million a year, per an American food outlet.

t055.text: It said losses might hit $30 million a year by 2015.

t056.text: Don't fret for the tyre firm. That year its revenue topped 20 billion euros.

t057.text: If the book can't pay, where's the money from?

t058.text: Also in 2011, Korea's tourism agency sought a Seoul edition.

t061.text: From 2016 it rolled out Asian editions.

t062.text: Oddly, Thailand needed no chasing: the cabinet budgeted it.

t064.text: But note its use: tourism promotion tied to the guide,

t065.text: not all paid to Michelin. How much went into its pocket?

t067.text: That year, a Michelin executive told The Washington Post plainly:

t068.text: Some governments sponsor it for tourism.

t069.text: The same article, as that food outlet retold it, also said: American cities never paid.

t070.text: Remember that; it gets funny. So what did the bill look like?

t071.text: The answer: Korea's parliament audit, October 2017.

t073.text: His name is Song Ki-seok. The contract he pressed: the agency would pay Michelin about 2 billion won

t074.text: through 2020. That's the lawmaker's claim; officials wouldn't give amounts.

t076.text: The allegation: money to get the guide published in Korea.

t077.text: It was about publishing, not anyone's star.

t078.text: But that's not the oddest. In that report, an owner said someone pitched consulting

t079.text: to land a star. She signed, then quit for financial reasons.

t080.text: Michelin denied any ties to him.

t081.text: I thought the story ended there. But the consulting saga had a sequel.

t082.text: Two years on, Korean public TV said some paid consulting fees and got stars.

t083.text: One owner's complaint: she was asked 50 million won a year;

t084.text: she refused and wasn't listed. Note: her account.

t085.text: Michelin: no money for listings; its check found no evidence.

t086.text: Prosecutors' outcome, official or court rulings: I found none. Not found is not found.

t087.text: Remember "American cities never paid"? It lasted two years.

t088.text: In 2019, California's tourism chief told local radio himself:

t089.text: they paid $600,000 to grow the guide from the Bay Area to all of California.

t091.text: In December 2021, Thai tourism issued a release:

t092.text: the deal was extended five years, to 2026, with a report card

t093.text: saying foreign visitors' food spending had doubled in 2019.

t094.text: Remember: that's the payer grading its own work.

t095.text: In 2023 came Atlanta: a $1 million contract; one fact-check says it was for three years.

t096.text: That fact-check came from a Colorado paper, headlined: Did our cities pay?

t097.text: The paper's answer was one word: yes.

t098.text: Since 2023, the state and some towns each pay $70,000 to $100,000 a year.

t100.text: The paper was clear: the money guarantees no recognition, only that inspectors come.

t101.text: But a Boston Globe op-ed said towns that didn't pay were shut out.

t103.text: It says tourism partnerships don't affect ratings.

t104.text: Odder still, in 2025 an executive also said: it's costly, it needs partners.

t105.text: Part of the tourism money pays inspectors' travel.

t106.text: It's not over. Those bills are abroad. What about the spot you queued at?

t107.text: Taiwan is on this list too, and it went asking.

t108.text: Global Views: the tourism bureau tried 8 years for the March 2018 Taipei edition.

t110.text: PTS said the bureau spent over 10 million Taiwan dollars,

t111.text: for secret inspectors' visits and more, and called the book worth investing in.

t112.text: Yet CommonWealth then said Michelin paid evaluation costs. The split, I can't find.

t113.text: August 2024, the minister told a food expo:

t114.text: Michelin agreed to add two more areas.

t115.text: Note his verb: agreed. It sounds like something the other side must OK.

t116.text: Odder: next year came three, not two: New Taipei, Hsinchu County and City.

t117.text: The agency calls it a ten-year plan, a planned government milestone.

t118.text: So why the minister spoke: the book is on the government's report card.

t119.text: The agency's under the transport ministry. Tyre book, transport minister: fitting, I'd say.

t122.text: Online there are bigger numbers, sourced to opinion or rumour.

t123.text: The ministry gave no amount either. So I leave this blank, no guess.

t124.text: Back to the ceremony. Money was paid. Did stars follow?

t125.text: This year Taiwan has 61 starred restaurants across seven cities,

t126.text: but the stars landed in only five places. New Taipei and Hsinchu City got none.

t127.text: Tainan's more curious: selected since 2022, its first starred place came only this year.

t128.text: And it was under a year old.

t129.text: If stars follow money, why would Tainan wait 4 years?

t130.text: Of course, it can't prove all. Judging is unseen.

t131.text: But my view: equating tourism money with stars doesn't hold up on this record.

t132.text: Okay, back to the question: why do cities pay for a free booklet?

t133.text: Remember the inspectors who pay their bills? That's my answer.

t134.text: Some believe that's what makes a star valuable, and why cities will pay.

t136.text: One: inviting it in, often tourism money.

t137.text: Two: inspectors' meals, paid by them, Michelin says.

t138.text: Yet it also says tourism money partly pays inspectors' trips; it needs partners.

t140.text: In the records I could find, neither bill says stars can be bought.

t141.text: But there were claims and a complaint; Michelin denies it. Not found isn't none.

t142.text: From the copy under a workbench to the minister's stage this year,

t143.text: who pays for this book keeps changing; what doesn't is whether you trust it.

t146.text: Comment below: would you detour for a star or a Bib Gourmand?

t147.text: This channel covers only what's on record. Subscribe and dig in with me.
